6.2: Starting out of her musing, she gave meaning to words she had been holding in her mind, meaningless, for a long stretch of time. “Someone had blundered”—the line from Tennyson’s “The Charge of the Light Brigade.” She fixed her shortsighted eyes on her husband, who was now bearing down on her, and gazed steadily until, as he came close, she could see (the jingle paired itself off in her head) that something had happened; someone had blundered. But she could not for the life of her think what.
6.3: He shivered; he quivered. It had all been shattered, destroyed: all his vanity, all his pleasure in his own splendor as he rode, fell as a thunderbolt, fierce as a hawk, at the head of his men through the valley of death. Stormed at by shot and shell, boldly we rode and well, flashed through the valley of death, volleyed and thundered—only to charge headlong into Lily Briscoe and William Bankes. He quivered; he shivered.
6.4: Not for the world would she have spoken to him. She knew the signs: his eyes turned away, and a curious gathering-in of his whole person, as if he were wrapping himself up and needed privacy in which to get his balance back. They told her he was outraged and in anguish. She stroked James’s head; she passed on to him what she felt for her husband. As she watched him color the white dress shirt of a gentleman in the Army and Navy Stores catalogue yellow with his chalk, she thought what a delight it would be to her if he turned out to be a great artist; and why shouldn’t he? He had a splendid forehead. Then, looking up as her husband passed her once more, she was relieved to find that the ruin was veiled. Domestic life had won; habit was crooning its soothing rhythm. So when he stopped deliberately at the window as his turn came round again, and bent down, teasing and whimsical, to tickle James’s bare calf with a sprig of something, she scolded him lightly for having sent off “that poor young man,” Charles Tansley. Tansley had had to go in and write his dissertation, he said.
6.5: “James will have to write _his_ dissertation one of these days,” he added ironically, flicking his sprig.
6.6: Hating his father, James brushed away the tickling spray with which his father was teasing his youngest son’s bare leg, in that way of his that was a mix of sternness and humor.
6.7: Mrs. Ramsay said she was trying to finish these wretched stockings so she could send them to Sorley’s little boy tomorrow.
6.8: There wasn’t the slightest chance in the world that they could go to the Lighthouse tomorrow, Mr. Ramsay snapped out irritably.
6.9: How did he know? she asked. The wind often changed.
6.10: It enraged him, the extraordinary irrationality of what she had just said, the folly of the female mind. He had ridden through the valley of death, had been shattered, had shivered; and now here she was defying the facts, letting his children hope for something utterly impossible—telling lies, in effect. He stamped on the stone step. “Damn you,” he said. Yet what had she actually said? Only that tomorrow might be fine. And so it might.
6.11: Not with the barometer falling and the wind due west.
6.12: To her it was a horrible outrage against human decency: to pursue the truth with so astonishing a disregard for other people’s feelings, to rip apart the thin veils of civilization so wantonly, so brutally. She gave no answer. Dazed and blinded, she bowed her head, as though letting the pelting of jagged hail, the soaking of dirty water, splash all over her without one word of reproach. There was nothing to be said.
6.13: He stood by her in silence. At last, very humbly, he said that he would walk over and ask the Coastguards, if she liked.
6.14: There was nobody she revered as she revered him.
6.15: She was perfectly willing to take his word for it, she said. It only meant they wouldn’t need to cut sandwiches—nothing more. Being a woman, she naturally had people coming to her all day long with one thing or another; this one wanted this, that one wanted that; the children were growing up; she often felt she was nothing but a sponge, soaked through with human emotions. And then he said, Damn you. He said, It must rain. He said, It won’t rain; and at once a Heaven of safety opened in front of her. There was no one she revered more. She wasn’t good enough to tie his shoelaces, she felt.
6.16: Already ashamed of that outburst, of the way he had waved his hands while charging at the head of his troops, Mr. Ramsay gave his son’s bare legs one more rather sheepish prod. Then, as though she had given him permission, he plunged off into the evening air. The movement struck his wife as oddly like the great sea lion at the Zoo, who tumbles over backward once he has swallowed his fish and flounders away, so that the water in the tank slops from one side to the other. The air was already thinning; it was drawing the substance out of the leaves and hedges, but, as if to make up for it, it gave the roses and pinks a luster they had lacked all day.
6.17: “Someone had blundered,” he said again, striding off, up and down the terrace.
6.18: How extraordinarily his tone had changed, though! It was like the cuckoo—“in June he gets out of tune”—as though he were trying out, groping toward, some phrase to suit a new mood, and, with nothing but this one to hand, made do with it, cracked as it was. Yet it sounded absurd, “Someone had blundered,” spoken that way, almost like a question, with no conviction at all, in a singsong voice. Mrs. Ramsay couldn’t help smiling, and before long, sure enough, pacing up and down, he hummed it, let it go, and went quiet.
6.19: He was safe; his privacy had been given back to him. He paused to light his pipe and glanced once at his wife and son in the window. You know how, on an express train, you lift your eyes from a page and see a farm, a tree, a huddle of cottages, as if they were a picture illustrating the printed words, a confirmation of them, and you go back to your book strengthened and content. Just so, without his really making out either his son or his wife, the sight of them gave him strength and contentment, and blessed his effort to reach a perfectly clear grasp of the problem that now absorbed the energies of his splendid mind.
6.20: It was a splendid mind. Suppose thought is like a piano keyboard, divided into so many notes, or like the alphabet, set out in twenty-six letters in order. Then his splendid mind could run through those letters one after another, firmly and accurately, with no trouble at all, until it arrived at, let us say, the letter Q. He reached Q. Hardly anyone in the whole of England ever gets to Q. Pausing a moment here by the stone urn with the geraniums in it, he caught sight of his wife and son together in the window, but far, far off now, like children gathering shells, divinely innocent, busy with small trifles at their feet, and somehow wholly unprotected against a doom that he could see coming. They needed his protection; he gave it to them. But what about after Q? What comes next? Beyond Q lie a number of letters, and the last of them can barely be seen by mortal eyes; it glimmers red, far away. Z is reached only once in a generation, by one man. Still, getting to R would be something. Here, at least, was Q. At Q he dug in his heels. Of Q he was certain. Q he could prove. If Q, then, is Q—R—At this point he knocked the ash out of his pipe with two or three ringing taps against the ram’s horn that formed the urn’s handle, and carried on. “Then R …” He steeled himself. He clenched himself.
6.21: Then came to his aid the qualities that would have saved a ship’s crew adrift on a scorching sea with a flask of water and six biscuits—endurance and fairness, foresight, devotion, skill. Well then, R is—what is R?
6.22: Like the leathery eyelid of a lizard, a shutter flickered down over his intense gaze and hid the letter R. In that flash of dark he could hear people saying it—that he was a failure, that R was beyond him. He would never get to R. Once more, on to R. R——
6.23: Once again the qualities came to his aid that, on some desolate expedition across the frozen solitudes of the Polar regions, would have made him the leader, the guide, the counselor—the one whose temper, neither hopeful nor gloomy, looks calmly at what lies ahead and meets it. R——
6.24: Again the lizard’s eye flickered. The veins stood out on his forehead. The geranium in the urn leapt startlingly into view, and there among its leaves, whether he wanted to or not, he could see that old, obvious division of men into two kinds. On one side were the steady ones, plodding and persevering with superhuman strength, who go through the whole alphabet in order, all twenty-six letters, beginning to end. On the other were the gifted, the inspired, who by some miracle take in all the letters at once, in a single flash—the way of genius. Genius he did not have; he made no claim to it. But he had, or might have had, the power to go through every letter from A to Z, accurately and in order. In the meantime, he was stuck on Q. Onward, then—on to R.
6.25: Over him crept feelings worthy of a leader who, with the snow now beginning to fall and mist closing over the mountaintop, knows he must lie down and die before morning. They faded the color of his eyes, and even in the two minutes it took him to walk the length of the terrace, they gave him the bleached look of shriveled old age. But he would not die lying down. He would find some crag of rock, and there, with his eyes on the storm, straining to the last to see through the darkness, he would die on his feet. R he would never reach.
6.26: He stood stock-still by the urn, the geranium spilling over its rim. After all, he asked himself, out of a thousand million men, how many ever get to Z? Surely the leader of a forlorn hope has the right to ask that, and to answer, without betraying the expedition following him, “One, perhaps.” One in a generation. Should he be blamed, then, for not being that one? so long as he has worked honestly, given everything in his power, until there is nothing left to give? And how long will his fame last? Even a dying hero may be forgiven for wondering, before he dies, how men will talk of him when he is gone. Perhaps his fame will last two thousand years. And what are two thousand years? (asked Mr. Ramsay ironically, staring at the hedge). What indeed, if you gaze down from a mountaintop across the long wastes of the ages? The very stone your boot kicks aside will outlast Shakespeare. His own small light would shine for a year or two, not very brightly, and would then be swallowed up in some larger light, and that in a larger one still. (He peered into the darkness, into the tangle of twigs.) So who could blame the leader of that forlorn party—which has, after all, climbed high enough to see the waste of the years and the stars perishing—if, before death stiffens his limbs so that he can no longer move, he lifts his numb fingers to his brow a little self-consciously and squares his shoulders, so that the search party, when it comes, will find him dead at his post, a fine figure of a soldier? Mr. Ramsay squared his shoulders and stood very straight beside the urn.
6.27: If he stands like that for a moment, dwelling on fame, on search parties, on the cairns of stones that grateful followers will heap over his bones, who will blame him? And last of all, who will blame the leader of the doomed expedition if, after venturing to the very limit, spending his strength down to the final ounce, and falling asleep with little care whether he ever wakes, he now feels a pricking in his toes and realizes that he is alive—and that, on the whole, he doesn’t mind being alive, but wants sympathy, and whisky, and someone to hear the story of his sufferings right away? Who will blame him? Who will not be secretly glad when the hero lays his armor aside, and pauses by the window, and gazes at his wife and son? They are very far away at first, then little by little they draw nearer and nearer, until lips and book and head are plain before him, though still lovely and strange to him after the intensity of his isolation, and the waste of the ages, and the perishing of the stars. And when at last he slips his pipe into his pocket and bows his magnificent head before her—who will blame him for paying homage to the beauty of the world?

7.0: But his son hated him. James hated him for coming up to them, for stopping and looking down at them; for interrupting them; for the lofty exaltation of his gestures; for his magnificent head; for his demands and his egotism (for there he stood, insisting that they attend to him). Most of all, though, he hated the twang and twitter of his father’s emotion, which quivered all around them and upset the perfect simplicity and good sense of the way things were between him and his mother. He stared hard at the page, hoping that would make his father move on; he pointed his finger at a word, hoping to win back his mother’s attention, which, he knew with anger, wavered the moment his father stopped. But no. Nothing would make Mr. Ramsay move on. There he stood, demanding sympathy.
7.1: Mrs. Ramsay had been sitting loosely, with her son folded in her arm. She braced herself, and, turning halfway round, seemed to raise herself with an effort, and then at once to send pouring straight up into the air a shower of energy, a column of spray. At the same time she looked vivid and alive, as though every energy she had were being fused into power, burning and lighting everything up (though she sat quietly, picking up her stocking again). And into this delicious fruitfulness, this fountain and spray of life, the fatal sterility of the male drove itself like a beak of brass, barren and bare. He wanted sympathy. He was a failure, he said. Mrs. Ramsay’s needles flashed. Never taking his eyes off her face, Mr. Ramsay said again that he was a failure. She blew the words back at him. “Charles Tansley …” she said. But he needed more than that. What he wanted was sympathy: to be reassured, first of all, that he was a genius, and then to be drawn inside the circle of life, warmed and comforted, to have his senses given back to him, his barrenness made fruitful, and every room in the house filled with life—the drawing room; the kitchen behind it; the bedrooms above the kitchen; and past those, the nurseries. They must be furnished; they must be full of life.
7.2: Charles Tansley considered him the greatest metaphysician of the day, she said. But he needed more than that. He needed sympathy. He needed to be told that he, too, lived at the heart of life; that he was needed; not just here, but everywhere in the world. Needles flashing, upright and sure of herself, she conjured up drawing room and kitchen and made them all glow; she invited him to be at ease there, to come and go, to enjoy himself. She laughed; she knitted. James stood very stiffly between her knees and felt all her strength blaze up only to be swallowed and put out by the beak of brass, the parched scimitar of the male, which struck without mercy, over and over, demanding sympathy.
7.3: He was a failure, he said again. Well, look, then; feel, then. Her needles flashing, glancing all around—out of the window, into the room, at James himself—she reassured him past any shadow of doubt, with her laugh, her poise, her capability (the way a nurse carrying a lamp through a dark room calms a fretful child), that it was real: the house was full; the garden was blossoming. If he trusted her completely, nothing would harm him; however deep he buried himself, or however high he climbed, never for a second would he be without her. And as she boasted like this of her power to enfold and protect, there was hardly a shell of her own self left for her to recognize herself by; it had all been poured out and spent. And James, standing stiffly between her knees, felt her rise up like a fruit tree full of rosy flowers, thick with leaves and dancing branches, and into it the beak of brass, the parched scimitar of his father, that egotistical man, plunged and struck, demanding sympathy.
7.4: At last, filled with her words like a child who falls asleep contented, he looked at her with humble gratitude, restored and renewed, and said he would go for a stroll; he would go and watch the children play cricket. Off he went.
7.5: All at once Mrs. Ramsay seemed to fold up on herself, one petal closing inside another, and the whole fabric collapsed on itself, worn out. She had just strength enough to move her finger across the page of Grimm’s fairy tale, in an exquisite giving-way to exhaustion. And through her there throbbed the rapture of successful creation, like the pulse in a spring that has stretched to its widest and now softly stops beating.
7.6: As he walked away, every beat of this pulse seemed to enclose her and her husband together, and to give each of them the comfort that two different notes, one high and one low, seem to give each other when they are struck at once and blend. But as the resonance faded, and she went back to the Fairy Tale, Mrs. Ramsay felt not just tired in body (she always felt this afterward, never at the time); her physical tiredness was also tinged with some faintly unpleasant feeling that had a different source. Not that she knew exactly what it came from as she read aloud the story of the Fisherman’s Wife. Nor would she let herself put her discontent into words when she saw—at the turn of the page, when she paused and heard, dully, ominously, a wave fall—what its source was. It was this. She disliked feeling, even for a second, that she was finer than her husband; and, beyond that, she could not stand being less than entirely sure, when she spoke to him, that what she said was true. The universities and the people who wanted him, the lectures and the books, and how supremely important they all were—none of that did she doubt for a moment. What unsettled her was the relationship between them, and the way he came to her like that, in the open, where anyone could see. Because then people said he depended on her, when they must surely know that he was by far the more important of the two, and that what she gave the world was nothing next to what he gave it. But then there was the other thing too: that she could not tell him the truth. She was afraid, say, about the greenhouse roof and how much it would cost to repair, fifty pounds perhaps; and about his books, afraid he might guess what she half suspected, that his latest book was not quite his best (she had picked that up from William Bankes); and then there were the small everyday things she hid, and the children noticing, and the weight it put on them. All this took away from the whole joy, the pure joy, of the two notes sounding together, and made the sound die in her ear now with a dreary flatness.
7.7: There was a shadow across the page; she looked up. It was Augustus Carmichael shuffling by—just now, of all moments, when it was painful to be reminded that human relationships fall short, that even the most perfect one had flaws and could not survive the scrutiny that she, loving her husband and having an instinct for truth, turned on it; when it was painful to feel herself found guilty of unworthiness, and held back from doing what she was meant to do by these lies, these exaggerations. It was at this moment, while she was fretting so ignobly in the wake of her exaltation, that Mr. Carmichael came shuffling by in his yellow slippers, and some demon in her made her call out to him as he passed,

8.0: He made no answer. He took opium. According to the children, it had stained his beard yellow. Perhaps it had. What was plain to her was that the poor man was unhappy, and that he came to them every year to escape; and still, every year, she felt the same thing: he did not trust her. She would say, “I’m going into town. Can I get you stamps, paper, tobacco?” and feel him flinch. He did not trust her. His wife was to blame. She remembered the wicked way his wife had treated him, which had turned her, Mrs. Ramsay, to steel and adamant right there in that horrid little room in St. John’s Wood, when she had watched with her own eyes as that hateful woman turned him out of the house. He was untidy; he spilled things on his coat; he had all the tedious habits of an old man with nothing in the world to do; and she turned him out of the room. In her hateful way she said, “Now, Mrs. Ramsay and I want to have a little talk together,” and Mrs. Ramsay could see, as clearly as if they were before her eyes, the endless miseries of his life. Had he enough money for tobacco? Did he have to ask his wife for it? Half a crown? Eighteen pence? Oh, she could not bear to think of the small humiliations that woman put him through. And always now (she could not guess why, unless it came from that woman somehow) he shrank away from her. He never confided in her. Yet what more could she have done? A sunny room had been set aside for him. The children were kind to him. Not once had she shown any sign that he was unwelcome. In fact she went out of her way to be friendly. Do you want stamps, do you want tobacco? Here’s a book you might enjoy, and so on. And after all—after all (at this point, without being aware of it, she drew herself up, and the sense of her own beauty, so seldom present to her, came to her now)—after all, she did not usually find it hard to make people like her. There was George Manning, for example; Mr. Wallace; famous men though they were, they would come to see her in the evening, quietly, and talk with her alone by her fire. She could not help knowing that she carried the torch of her beauty with her wherever she went; she carried it high into every room she walked into. And after all, however much she might veil it, and shrink from the monotonous bearing it forced on her, her beauty showed. She had been admired. She had been loved. She had walked into rooms where people sat mourning. Tears had been shed in front of her. Men, and women too, had set aside the multitude of things in their lives and allowed themselves, with her, the relief of simplicity. It wounded her that he should shrink from her. It hurt. And yet it was not a clean hurt, not a right one. That was what bothered her, coming as it did on top of her discontent with her husband: the feeling she had now—as Mr. Carmichael shuffled past, barely nodding in answer to her question, a book under his arm, in his yellow slippers—that she was under suspicion; that all this longing of hers to give, to help, was vanity. Was it for her own gratification that she wanted so instinctively to help, to give, so that people would say of her, “O Mrs. Ramsay! dear Mrs. Ramsay … Mrs. Ramsay, of course!” and need her, and send for her, and admire her? Wasn’t this what she secretly wanted? And so when Mr. Carmichael drew back from her, as he was doing at this very moment, slipping away to some corner where he did his acrostic puzzles endlessly, she felt not simply rebuffed in her instinct, but made aware of the pettiness of some part of herself, and of human relations—how flawed they are, how contemptible, how selfish, even at their best. Worn out and shabby, and presumably no longer (her cheeks were hollow, her hair was white) a sight to fill anyone’s eyes with joy, she had better give her mind to the story of the Fisherman and his Wife, and so calm that bundle of sensitiveness, her son James (none of her children was as sensitive as he was).
8.1: “The man’s heart grew heavy,” she read aloud, “and he did not want to go. ‘It is not right,’ he said to himself, but he went all the same. And when he reached the sea, the water was all purple and dark blue, and gray and thick, not green and yellow the way it had been, but it was still calm. And he stood there and said—”
8.2: Mrs. Ramsay could have wished her husband hadn’t picked that moment to stop. Why hadn’t he gone off to watch the children play cricket, as he’d said he would? But he said nothing; he looked; he nodded; he approved; he moved on. Before him he saw the hedge that had so many times rounded off a pause, signaled a conclusion; he saw his wife and child; he saw once more the urns with their trailing red geraniums, which had so often decorated his processes of thought and which bore them written up among their leaves, like scraps of paper you scribble notes on in the rush of reading. Seeing all this, he slid smoothly into speculation prompted by an article in _The Times_ on how many Americans visit Shakespeare’s house each year. Had Shakespeare never existed, he asked, would the world be much different from the way it is now? Does civilization advance because of great men? Is the ordinary person better off now than under the Pharaohs? And yet, he asked himself, is the ordinary person’s lot the right yardstick for measuring civilization? Possibly not. Possibly the greatest good depends on there being a slave class. The man who operates the lift in the Underground will always be necessary. He found the thought distasteful. He tossed his head. To escape it, he would find a way to take the arts down a peg. He would argue that the world exists for the ordinary person; that the arts are just ornament laid on top of human life; they do not express it. Nor does life need Shakespeare. Without knowing quite why he wanted to run Shakespeare down and to rescue the man who stands forever in the door of the lift, he snapped a leaf off the hedge. All this would have to be served up for the young men at Cardiff next month, he thought; out here on his terrace he was only foraging and picnicking (he tossed away the leaf he had picked so peevishly), like a man leaning down from his horse to gather a bunch of roses, or filling his pockets with nuts as he ambles comfortably through the lanes and fields of the countryside he has known since he was a boy. All of it was familiar: this bend, that stile, that path across the fields. He would spend hours this way in the evenings, with his pipe, thinking his way up and down and in and out of the old familiar lanes and commons, which were all dotted with the history of that campaign over there, the life of this statesman here, with poems and anecdotes, and with figures too, this thinker, that soldier; everything brisk and clear. But eventually the lane, the field, the common, the fruitful nut tree and the flowering hedge brought him to that further bend in the road where he always dismounted, tied his horse to a tree, and went on alone, on foot. He came to the edge of the lawn and gazed out over the bay below.
8.3: It was his fate, his particular nature, whether he liked it or not, to come out like this onto a spit of land that the sea is slowly eating away, and to stand there by himself like some desolate seabird. It was his power, his gift, to throw off everything superfluous all at once, shrinking and dwindling until he looked barer and felt leaner, even in his body, yet without losing any of the intensity of his mind; and in that state to stand on his little ledge, facing the darkness of human ignorance—how we know nothing, and the sea eats away the ground we stand on. That was his fate, his gift. But when he dismounted he had cast off every gesture and frill, all his trophies of nuts and roses, and had shrunk until he had forgotten not only his fame but his very name; and even in that desolation he stayed alert, sparing no phantom, indulging in no vision. And it was in this guise that he inspired a deep reverence, and pity, and gratitude as well, in William Bankes (now and then), in Charles Tansley (fawningly), and in his wife now, as she looked up and saw him standing at the edge of the lawn. It was the kind of gratitude that a stake, driven into the bed of a channel, with gulls perching on it and waves beating against it, inspires in boatloads of merrymakers, for the duty it has taken on of marking the channel out there in the floods, alone.
8.4: “But the father of eight children has no choice. …” He broke off his half-audible muttering, turned, sighed, lifted his eyes, looked for the figure of his wife reading stories to the little boy, and filled his pipe. He turned his back on the sight of human ignorance and human fate and the sea eating the ground we stand on—a sight which, had he been able to hold his gaze on it, might have led somewhere. And he took comfort in trifles so slight, next to the grand theme he had just been facing, that he was inclined to skip over that comfort, to disown it, as though for an honest man to be caught being happy in a world of misery were the most shameful crime of all. It was true: most of the time he was happy; he had his wife; he had his children; in six weeks he had promised to talk “some nonsense” to the young men of Cardiff about Locke, Hume, Berkeley, and the causes of the French Revolution. But all this, and the pleasure he took in it—in the phrases he turned, in the ardor of the young, in his wife’s beauty, in the tributes that came to him from Swansea, Cardiff, Exeter, Southampton, Kidderminster, Oxford, Cambridge—all of it had to be made light of and hidden under the words “talking nonsense,” because, in effect, he had not done the thing he might have done. It was a disguise. It was where a man took refuge who was afraid to own his own feelings, who could not say, This is what I like—this is what I am. And William Bankes and Lily Briscoe found it rather pitiful and distasteful; they wondered why such concealments were needed; why he always needed praise; why a man so brave in his thinking should be so timid in his living; how oddly he was both venerable and laughable at once.
8.5: Lily suspected that teaching and preaching are more than any human being can manage. (She was packing up her things.) If you are lifted up high, you are bound to come down with a crash somehow. Mrs. Ramsay gave him what he wanted too easily. And then the change must be so jarring, Lily said. He comes in from his books and finds us all playing games and chattering nonsense. Just think what a change that is from the things he thinks about, she said.
8.6: He was bearing down on them. Now he had stopped dead and was standing, silent, looking out at the sea. Now he had turned away again.
